external.description:
Some ideas need money to take off. Others need the right people, or simply an opportunity to show their worth. Yet, for many aspiring founders, researchers, and professionals, getting access to these resources can be just as difficult as developing the ideas themselves.

Currently, several organisations are offering a way around that through fellowships that go beyond conventional funding. From $50,000 in unrestricted support for independent builders to research opportunities at Anthropic, these programmes provide financial backing, mentorship, technical expertise, and access to networks that could help participants take their work further.

Whether you're looking to turn scientific research into a business or even gain practical experience in an emerging field, here are six fellowships worth exploring, including what they offer, who can apply, and the deadlines to keep in mind.

## 1. Breakthrough Energy Fellows (BE Fellows) – Cohort 7

Scientists, researchers, and entrepreneurs developing technologies that could help tackle climate change can apply for Cohort 7 of the Breakthrough Energy Fellows programme.

The fellowship supports early-stage innovators working to turn promising scientific discoveries into commercially viable climate technologies, particularly those that may struggle to attract conventional venture capital at an early stage.

Selected Innovator Fellows receive up to $500,000 in research and development support, alongside hands-on technical guidance, mentorship, and access to a global network of industry experts.

The programme also connects participants with commercial and technical expertise to help them address challenges around product development, market readiness, and scaling their innovations.

It is particularly relevant for founders developing breakthrough technologies in areas such as clean energy, manufacturing, transportation, and other sectors critical to reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

  * **Programme:** One-year Innovator Fellowship with up to $500k R&D support and extensive in-kind resources.
  * **Focus:** Early-stage climate/hard-tech commercialisation.
  * **Deadline:** 2 November 2026.



## 2. Activate Fellowship (U.S. Cohort 2027)

Science and engineering founders looking to turn their research into commercially viable businesses can apply for Activate's two-year fellowship, which provides more than $300,000 in financial support without taking equity.

Selected fellows receive a $100,000 annual living stipend, $100,000 in research and development support, and $12,000 annually for travel and professional development. The package also includes health insurance, relocation assistance, mentorship, and entrepreneurial training.

Beyond the financial support, participants gain access to technical facilities, industry experts, and a community of science-based entrepreneurs working to bring their technologies to market.

Applicants must have at least a bachelor's degree and four years of relevant research or engineering experience. They should also be commercialising a hardware-based technology for the first time and have raised less than $2 million from non-government sources.

The programme requires applicants to be legally authorised to work in the United States.

  * Programme: Two-year fellowship offering over $300,000 in support without taking equity.
  * Eligibility: First-time science and engineering founders with relevant technical experience and US work authorisation.
  * Location: United States.
  * Deadline: October 30, 2026.



## 3. Basis Fellowship

The programme provides selected individuals with $50,000 in unrestricted funding without taking equity, requiring a pitch deck, or imposing conventional reporting obligations. Mostly, it is set up for independent builders, engineers, scientists, and entrepreneurs who need financial support to pursue an ambitious idea.

Unlike startup accelerators, Basis does not require applicants to have an established company or follow a particular commercial development path. Fellows have the freedom to pursue projects they consider important, whether that involves developing new technology, conducting research, or experimenting with an unconventional idea.

The application takes approximately 10 minutes, and applicants who are not selected for the main fellowship may still be considered for a discretionary $3,000 award.

Applications are accepted on a rolling basis, making it an option for builders who need funding but may not fit the requirements of conventional startup programmes.

  * Programme: $50,000 in unrestricted funding with no equity requirement.
  * Eligibility: Engineers, scientists, operators, entrepreneurs, and independent builders.
  * Application: Approximately 10 minutes.
  * Deadline: Rolling applications.



## 4. Palantir Meritocracy Fellowship

The programme is designed for applicants who have demonstrated independent learning, problem-solving ability, or technical achievement and believe a conventional college experience may not offer the challenges they seek. As a four-month programme, it gives exceptional graduating high school seniors an opportunity to develop their intellectual and technical abilities while gaining practical experience at the software company.

Fellows begin with five weeks of intensive learning, examining questions around Western civilisation, American institutions, and Palantir's mission. During this period, they also engage with professionals across engineering, product, security, deployment, and operations.

Participants subsequently join Palantir's development or forward-deployed engineering teams, where they work alongside full-time engineers on real customer problems, build software, and gain practical experience in deployment.

Strong performance during the fellowship can also create an opportunity to interview for a full-time position at Palantir.

  * Programme: Four-month fellowship combining intellectual development and practical software engineering experience.
  * Eligibility: Exceptional graduating high school seniors with demonstrated technical ability and independent initiative.
  * Location: United States.
  * Application: Rolling.

Beyond the financial support, participants gain access to technical facilities, industry experts, and a community of science-based entrepreneurs working to bring their technologies to market.

The programme provides selected individuals with $50,000 in unrestricted funding without taking equity, requiring a pitch deck, or imposing conventional reporting obligations. Mostly, it is set up for independent builders, engineers, scientists, and entrepreneurs who need financial support to pursue an ambitious idea. 

Unlike startup accelerators, Basis does not require applicants to have an established company or follow a particular commercial development path. Fellows have the freedom to pursue projects they consider important, whether that involves developing new technology, conducting research, or experimenting with an unconventional idea. 

The application takes approximately 10 minutes, and applicants who are not selected for the main fellowship may still be considered for a discretionary $3,000 award. 

Applications are accepted on a rolling basis, making it an option for builders who need funding but may not fit the requirements of conventional startup programmes.

  • Eligibility: Engineers, scientists, operators, entrepreneurs, and independent builders. 
  • Application: Approximately 10 minutes. 
  • Deadline: Rolling applications.

The programme is designed for applicants who have demonstrated independent learning, problem-solving ability, or technical achievement and believe a conventional college experience may not offer the challenges they seek. As a four-month programme, it gives exceptional graduating high school seniors an opportunity to develop their intellectual and technical abilities while gaining practical experience at the software company. 

Fellows begin with five weeks of intensive learning, examining questions around Western civilisation, American institutions, and Palantir's mission. During this period, they also engage with professionals across engineering, product, security, deployment, and operations. 

Participants subsequently join Palantir's development or forward-deployed engineering teams, where they work alongside full-time engineers on real customer problems, build software, and gain practical experience in deployment. 

Strong performance during the fellowship can also create an opportunity to interview for a full-time position at Palantir.

  • Eligibility: Exceptional graduating high school seniors with demonstrated technical ability and independent initiative. 
  • Location: United States. 
  • Application: Rolling.

record.text: Startups across Africa, the Middle East and Israel raised a combined $101.9 million this week, led by Pluto Security $42 million

external.description:
Startups across Africa, the Middle East and Israel raised a combined $101.9 million this week, based on disclosed funding rounds tracked by Techloy, with investor capital flowing mostly into AI cybersecurity and electric fleets. Pluto Security’s $42 million and MAX’s $29 million made up about 70% of the total.

## **The Week’s Largest Startup Funding Rounds**

Here are the biggest disclosed startup funding rounds across Africa, the Middle East and Israel this week.

### **1. Pluto Security, $42M, AI Cybersecurity, Israel**

Pluto Security makes software that shows companies which AI tools their staff use and flags risky ones. The Israeli startup came out of stealth with $42 million: an approximate $34 million Series A led by Jump Capital and an $8.5 million seed led by TLV Partners. It will fund product development, research and US expansion.

### **2. MAX, $29M, Electric Mobility, Nigeria**

MAX is a Lagos company that gives drivers electric two-wheelers on subscription. Climate fintech Nithio backed it, taking its Series B3 round to $29 million, but didn’t say how much it put in. The money goes toward more two-wheelers from Spiro and NOVR and a bigger charging and battery-swap network.

### **3. Autobia, $12M, Autotech, Saudi Arabia**

Autobia runs a B2B marketplace where auto parts retailers and wholesalers in Saudi Arabia buy from verified suppliers. Artal Capital led its $12 million Series A, with Aljazira Capital and Wa’ed Ventures joining. The money goes toward wider reach across the country, stronger logistics and fulfilment, and its pricing technology and inventory financing.

### **4. Bisedge, $11.2M, Electric Logistics, Mauritius**

Bisedge, founded in Lagos and now based in Mauritius, rents electric forklifts, reach trucks and tractors to businesses. Finnfund, Finland’s development financier, gave it a €10 million (about $11.2 million) long-term loan. The money goes toward growing its electric fleet and service operations, mainly in Nigeria and East Africa.

### **5. JustAd, $5M, Marketing Tech, UAE**

JustAd is a UAE-based platform where advertisers run campaigns on Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and Google Ads, and pay for ads later in instalments of up to 12 months. Angel investor Imad Jomaa put in $5 million. The money goes toward local teams, product changes for new markets and closer ties with ad platforms.

### **6. Solarise Africa, $1.12M, Clean Energy, Kenya**

Solarise Africa is a Nairobi-based company that designs, finances and maintains solar systems for businesses. EEP Africa gave it a €1 million (about $1.12 million) grant, and Solarise is adding €1 million in co-financing. The €2 million programme aims to deploy 3 megawatts of solar, battery storage and heat pumps in Uganda and Zambia.

### **7. Wisewell, $545K, Water Tech, UAE**

Wisewell makes smart water purifiers for homes and businesses. The Mohammed Bin Rashid Innovation Fund, a UAE government fund, gave it an AED 2 million (about $545,000) credit guarantee, which helps it borrow from banks without giving up equity. The backing goes toward capital spending, business development and research.

### **8. Vatar, $500K, Gaming, Nigeria**

Vatar is the company behind Lagos Life, a free browser game set in Lagos that passed 4 million players within a week of its October 1 release. It closed a $500,000 angel round at a $10 million valuation, with backing from Flutterwave CEO Olugbenga Agboola’s fund, Resilience17. The money goes toward product development, marketing and hiring.

record.text: Asian startups raised more than $350 million this week, with semiconductor engineering, robotics, electric mobility, AI and battery technology attracting the biggest investments.

external.description:
Asia’s startup funding remained strong this week, with more than $353.73 million flowing into companies across semiconductors, robotics, electric mobility, AI, quantum computing and clean energy. India accounted for several of the largest rounds, while Chinese and South Korean companies attracted capital for robotics and advanced manufacturing.

## The Week’s Biggest Startup Funding Rounds

Here are the most notable startup funding announcements across Asia this week, ranked from highest to lowest.

### /1. Tessolve Semiconductor, $75 Million, Semiconductor Engineering, India

Indian semiconductor engineering company Tessolve Semiconductor raised $75 million in a funding round led by Vector Line Capital, with participation from existing investors TPG and Novo Tellus Capital Partners.

The company will use the capital to pursue strategic acquisitions, expand its semiconductor engineering services and strengthen its global presence as demand grows for chip design, testing and validation services.

### /2. Zhejiang Sankai Electromechanical, $70 Million+, Robotics, China

Chinese manufacturer Zhejiang Sankai Electromechanical secured more than $70 million in Series B funding to expand its production capacity and advance its robotics technology.

The company is developing precision gear reducers for humanoid robots, a critical component that enables controlled movement. The investment will support manufacturing expansion and further development of its robotics components.

### /3. GreenCell Mobility, $35 Million, Electric Mobility, India

Indian electric bus platform GreenCell Mobility, part of the Eversource Capital portfolio, secured an equity investment of ₹330 crore (about $35 million) from Impact Fund Denmark.

The funding will support the deployment of approximately 4,500 electric buses in the company’s order book. GreenCell aims to expand its fleet beyond 5,000 buses across 105 Indian cities, strengthening its position in the country’s electric public transport market.

### /4. Scimplify, $25 Million, Advanced Manufacturing, India

Bengaluru-based Scimplify raised $25 million in a funding round led by Hitachi Ventures.

The company will use the capital to expand its critical metals processing operations, scale its semiconductor and battery chemicals businesses, and strengthen SciNode, its AI-powered manufacturing platform.

### /5. Hurotics, $18.6 Million, Wearable Robotics, South Korea

South Korean wearable robotics startup Hurotics raised approximately $18.6 million in Series A funding led by Atinum Investment.

The company plans to expand its medical rehabilitation products into overseas markets and develop wearable robots designed to help people walk and perform everyday activities. The investment will support its efforts to bring robotic assistance into rehabilitation and daily mobility.

### /6. Nobikan Artificial Intelligence Technology, $16.3 Million, AI Infrastructure, China

Hong Kong-listed Nobikan Artificial Intelligence Technology secured approximately $16.3 million through a post-IPO equity placement.

The company plans to invest in core AI research, AI agent platforms, model-as-a-service offerings and computing infrastructure as it expands its artificial intelligence capabilities.

### /7. Shenzhen Ruoyu Technology, $13.8 Million, Robotics AI, China

Chinese robotics startup Shenzhen Ruoyu Technology raised $13.8 million in a Pre-Series A funding round led by Sunway Communication.

Jinmu Capital, Qindao Capital, Huanghai Capital and Zhongchuang Capital also participated. The company will use the funding to advance its robotics intelligence technology, strengthen real-world data collection and accelerate commercialisation.

### /8. Mesa School of Business, $12.7 Million, EdTech, India

Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business raised $12.7 million (₹110 crore) in a Series A funding round co-led by Dharana Capital and existing investor Elevation Capital.

The company plans to integrate AI into its courses, introduce new programmes, strengthen its leadership team and expand partnerships with startups.

### /9. OQT, $10.5 Million, Quantum Computing, South Korea

South Korean quantum computing startup OQT secured $10.5 million in pre-Series A funding led by DSC Investment.

The company is developing error-tolerant quantum computers for industrial and research applications. The investment will support further development of its quantum computing systems and their potential commercial uses.

### /10. Spill Games, $10.5 Million, Mobile Gaming, India

Bengaluru-based mobile gaming startup Spill Games raised $10.5 million in a Series A funding round led by Elevation Capital. Existing investors Centre Court Capital and PeerCapital also participated.

The company develops casual, puzzle and hybrid-casual mobile games for international markets. It plans to use the capital to scale promising titles, develop new games, improve its technology and increase user acquisition.

### /11. MakeO, $10 Million, Dental Care, India

Indian dental care platform MakeO, the parent company of Singapore-based Zenyum, raised $10 million in a funding round led by Singularity AMC, with participation from funds and family offices.

Announced on 13 October 2026, the investment will support the group’s expansion across Asia, technology development and increased manufacturing capacity.

Jinmu Capital, Qindao Capital, Huanghai Capital and Zhongchuang Capital also participated. The company will use the funding to advance its robotics intelligence technology, strengthen real-world data collection and accelerate commercialisation.

### /8. Mesa School of Business, $12.7 Million, EdTech, India

Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business raised $12.7 million (₹110 crore) in a Series A funding round co-led by Dharana Capital and existing investor Elevation Capital.

The company plans to integrate AI into its courses, introduce new programmes, strengthen its leadership team and expand partnerships with startups.

### /9. OQT, $10.5 Million, Quantum Computing, South Korea

South Korean quantum computing startup OQT secured $10.5 million in pre-Series A funding led by DSC Investment.

The company is developing error-tolerant quantum computers for industrial and research applications. The investment will support further development of its quantum computing systems and their potential commercial uses.

### /10. Spill Games, $10.5 Million, Mobile Gaming, India

Bengaluru-based mobile gaming startup Spill Games raised $10.5 million in a Series A funding round led by Elevation Capital. Existing investors Centre Court Capital and PeerCapital also participated.

The company develops casual, puzzle and hybrid-casual mobile games for international markets. It plans to use the capital to scale promising titles, develop new games, improve its technology and increase user acquisition.

### /11. MakeO, $10 Million, Dental Care, India

Indian dental care platform MakeO, the parent company of Singapore-based Zenyum, raised $10 million in a funding round led by Singularity AMC, with participation from funds and family offices.

Announced on 13 October 2026, the investment will support the group’s expansion across Asia, technology development and increased manufacturing capacity.

record.text: Repeated Copilot Code of Conduct Blocks Are Preventing Legitimate Work

external.description: Hello, I am experiencing repeated and inconsistent Code of Conduct blocks while using Microsoft Copilot image generation for an unpublished multilingual creative project. The requests involve benign, fully clothed fictional character illustrations. Equivalent requests have sometimes generated successfully in English, been rejected after translation into Slovak, and then later generated successfully in Slovak without any meaningful change to the requested content. external.description:
Reports exported from several systems rarely use the same wording. One file says "North America", another says "America"; a department was renamed last quarter; a column header oscillates between "Total" and "Sum". Fixing this by hand has a second, quieter cost: after the edits nobody knows which cells were touched, so verification becomes a line-by-line comparison. A more practical approach is to let a script perform the replacement and color every changed cell at the same time, so the affected area is visible at a glance.

In Python this can be done with Spire.XLS for Python. Beyond plain string replacement, the library supports regular expression matching, numeric and formula lookup, and replacement that applies a new style in the same call, which covers most report-cleaning scenarios.

##  Why Do Find and Replace in a Script

  * **Auditable** : the result is written to a new file while the original stays untouched, so you can always compare before and after.
  * **Annotated** : replacing and highlighting happen in the same loop, so there is no separate pass to work out what changed.
  * **Repeatable** : the same rules apply to dozens of worksheets or files by adding one more loop.



##  Setting Up the Environment

Install the Spire.XLS library:



    pip install Spire.XLS


Then import the required modules in your script:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *


##  Finding and Replacing Text While Highlighting It

The worksheet-level `FindAllString()` returns a collection of every matching cell, and iterating that collection is enough to change the text and style one cell at a time. The example below replaces every "Total" with "Sum" and fills the affected cells in yellow:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *

    workbook = Workbook()
    workbook.LoadFromFile("Report.xlsx")
    worksheet = workbook.Worksheets[0]

    # Find all matching cells
    ranges = worksheet.FindAllString("Total", True, True)

    for range in ranges:
        # Assigning the text performs the replacement
        range.Text = "Sum"
        # Fill the cell yellow to mark the change
        range.Style.Color = Color.get_Yellow()

    workbook.SaveToFile("ReplaceAndHighlight.xlsx", ExcelVersion.Version2010)
    workbook.Dispose()


The three arguments of `FindAllString()` are the text to look for, whether the search is case-sensitive, and whether it must match a whole word. Passing `True, True` here means only a standalone "Total" with exactly that casing is replaced, so `total` and `Subtotal` are left alone. `range.Text` is both a read and a write property — assigning to it performs the replacement — while `range.Style.Color` controls the cell fill and `Color.get_Yellow()` is a predefined color from the enum.

##  Marking Matches Without Changing the Content

When reviewing data you often want to flag suspicious cells rather than modify them. In that case, skip the assignment inside the loop:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *

    workbook = Workbook()
    workbook.LoadFromFile("Data.xlsx")
    worksheet = workbook.Worksheets[0]

    ranges = worksheet.FindAllString("Area", False, False)

    for range in ranges:
        # Keep the original text, mark it with color only
        range.Style.Color = Color.get_Yellow()

    workbook.SaveToFile("Marked.xlsx", ExcelVersion.Version2013)
    workbook.Dispose()


Both flags are `False` here, so the search ignores case and does not require a whole-word match. "Area", "area", and "Area Code" are all highlighted.

##  Matching Complex Patterns with Regular Expressions

Regular expressions help when the data has no fixed literal form. `FindAllString()` has an overload with a fourth parameter; set it to `True` to enable regex matching:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *

    workbook = Workbook()
    workbook.LoadFromFile("FindTextByRegex.xlsx")
    worksheet = workbook.Worksheets[0]

    # Match every text that starts with North
    ranges = worksheet.FindAllString(".*North.", False, False, True)

    for range in ranges:
        range.Style.Color = Color.get_Yellow()

    workbook.SaveToFile("RegexHighlighted.xlsx", ExcelVersion.Version2013)
    workbook.Dispose()


The pattern follows .NET regular expression syntax, so `\d{4}` locates four-digit years and `^A.*` locates any text beginning with A. Combining a regex with highlighting is a quick way to circle the cells that break a naming convention in a sheet that mixes several formats.

##  Finding Numbers and Formulas

Non-text data has its own lookup methods:



    # Find the number 100; the second argument means "match the exact value"
    numberRanges = sheet.FindAllNumber(100, True)
    for range in numberRanges:
        print(range.RangeAddress)

    # Find cells that use a specific formula
    formulaRanges = sheet.FindAll("=SUM(A11,A12)", FindType.Formula, ExcelFindOptions.none)
    for range in formulaRanges:
        print(range.RangeAddress)


When the second argument of `FindAllNumber()` is `True`, only cells equal to that number match; with `False`, cells containing the number also match. `FindAll()` takes a `FindType` value — besides `Formula` it supports `Text`, `Number`, and `DateTime` — while `ExcelFindOptions.none` means no extra match options are applied. Unlike the earlier examples, these results are usually used for locating rather than editing: read `range.RangeAddress` inside the loop to get the cell reference, then act on it. A common follow-up is deleting the whole row:



    cr = sheet.FindString("Address", False, False)
    sheet.DeleteRow(cr.Row)


`FindString()` returns only the first match, which suits "handle it once" cases. Read the `Row` property from the result and pass it to `DeleteRow()` to remove the row that carries the keyword.

##  Applying a New Style During Replacement

When a replacement also has to update appearance, `ReplaceAll()` performs the content and style swap in a single call. It takes four arguments: the old text, the old style, the new text, and the new style.



    newStyle = workbook.Styles.Add("newStyle")
    newStyle.Font.FontName = "Arial Black"
    newStyle.Font.Size = 14

    cellRange = sheet.Range["D9"]
    oldStyle = cellRange.Style
    sheet.ReplaceAll("North America", oldStyle, "America", newStyle)


This replaces "North America" with "America" only in cells whose style matches cell `D9`, and applies `newStyle` (Arial Black, size 14) at the same time. Styles created with `workbook.Styles.Add()` can be reused, so for consistently formatted reports you can take the style from one sample cell and let `ReplaceAll()` filter by it, which avoids rewriting identical text elsewhere in the sheet.

##  Practical Tips

  * **Choose the match strength deliberately** : start with `False, False` to see the full set of matches, then tighten to a whole-word match once the data is confirmed clean.
  * **Log the addresses** : collect `range.RangeAddress` into a list or a log file during the loop to produce a change list after the replacement finishes.
  * **Keep a backup** : even though the script writes a new file, retain the original so the diff between the two versions stays available.
  * **Release resources** : call `workbook.Dispose()` after each workbook, and in batch jobs load, process, and release one file at a time.
  * **Work across worksheets** : `FindAllString()` operates on one worksheet, so for multi-sheet workbooks loop with `Worksheets.Count` and `get_Item(i)`.



##  Conclusion

This article covered several ways to find and replace data in Excel with Python: replacing text through `FindAllString()` and marking the results with `Style.Color`, matching complex patterns through the regex overload, locating numbers and formulas with `FindAllNumber()` and `FindAll()`, and applying a new style during replacement with `ReplaceAll()`. Combined, these operations form an auditable report-cleaning routine in which replacement and annotation happen in one pass.

Reports exported from several systems rarely use the same wording. One file says "North America", another says "America"; a department was renamed last quarter; a column header oscillates between "Total" and "Sum". Fixing this by hand has a second, quieter cost: after the edits nobody knows which cells were touched, so verification becomes a line-by-line comparison. A more practical approach is to let a script perform the replacement and color every changed cell at the same time, so the affected area is visible at a glance.

In Python this can be done with Spire.XLS for Python. Beyond plain string replacement, the library supports regular expression matching, numeric and formula lookup, and replacement that applies a new style in the same call, which covers most report-cleaning scenarios.

##  Why Do Find and Replace in a Script

  * **Auditable** : the result is written to a new file while the original stays untouched, so you can always compare before and after.
  * **Annotated** : replacing and highlighting happen in the same loop, so there is no separate pass to work out what changed.
  * **Repeatable** : the same rules apply to dozens of worksheets or files by adding one more loop.



##  Setting Up the Environment

Install the Spire.XLS library:



    pip install Spire.XLS


Then import the required modules in your script:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *


##  Finding and Replacing Text While Highlighting It

The worksheet-level `FindAllString()` returns a collection of every matching cell, and iterating that collection is enough to change the text and style one cell at a time. The example below replaces every "Total" with "Sum" and fills the affected cells in yellow:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *

    workbook = Workbook()
    workbook.LoadFromFile("Report.xlsx")
    worksheet = workbook.Worksheets[0]

    # Find all matching cells
    ranges = worksheet.FindAllString("Total", True, True)

    for range in ranges:
        # Assigning the text performs the replacement
        range.Text = "Sum"
        # Fill the cell yellow to mark the change
        range.Style.Color = Color.get_Yellow()

    workbook.SaveToFile("ReplaceAndHighlight.xlsx", ExcelVersion.Version2010)
    workbook.Dispose()


The three arguments of `FindAllString()` are the text to look for, whether the search is case-sensitive, and whether it must match a whole word. Passing `True, True` here means only a standalone "Total" with exactly that casing is replaced, so `total` and `Subtotal` are left alone. `range.Text` is both a read and a write property — assigning to it performs the replacement — while `range.Style.Color` controls the cell fill and `Color.get_Yellow()` is a predefined color from the enum.

##  Marking Matches Without Changing the Content

When reviewing data you often want to flag suspicious cells rather than modify them. In that case, skip the assignment inside the loop:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *

    workbook = Workbook()
    workbook.LoadFromFile("Data.xlsx")
    worksheet = workbook.Worksheets[0]

    ranges = worksheet.FindAllString("Area", False, False)

    for range in ranges:
        # Keep the original text, mark it with color only
        range.Style.Color = Color.get_Yellow()

    workbook.SaveToFile("Marked.xlsx", ExcelVersion.Version2013)
    workbook.Dispose()


Both flags are `False` here, so the search ignores case and does not require a whole-word match. "Area", "area", and "Area Code" are all highlighted.

##  Matching Complex Patterns with Regular Expressions

Regular expressions help when the data has no fixed literal form. `FindAllString()` has an overload with a fourth parameter; set it to `True` to enable regex matching:



    from spire.xls import *
    from spire.xls.common import *

    workbook = Workbook()
    workbook.LoadFromFile("FindTextByRegex.xlsx")
    worksheet = workbook.Worksheets[0]

    # Match every text that starts with North
    ranges = worksheet.FindAllString(".*North.", False, False, True)

    for range in ranges:
        range.Style.Color = Color.get_Yellow()

    workbook.SaveToFile("RegexHighlighted.xlsx", ExcelVersion.Version2013)
    workbook.Dispose()


The pattern follows .NET regular expression syntax, so `\d{4}` locates four-digit years and `^A.*` locates any text beginning with A. Combining a regex with highlighting is a quick way to circle the cells that break a naming convention in a sheet that mixes several formats.

##  Finding Numbers and Formulas

Non-text data has its own lookup methods:



    # Find the number 100; the second argument means "match the exact value"
    numberRanges = sheet.FindAllNumber(100, True)
    for range in numberRanges:
        print(range.RangeAddress)

    # Find cells that use a specific formula
    formulaRanges = sheet.FindAll("=SUM(A11,A12)", FindType.Formula, ExcelFindOptions.none)
    for range in formulaRanges:
        print(range.RangeAddress)


When the second argument of `FindAllNumber()` is `True`, only cells equal to that number match; with `False`, cells containing the number also match. `FindAll()` takes a `FindType` value — besides `Formula` it supports `Text`, `Number`, and `DateTime` — while `ExcelFindOptions.none` means no extra match options are applied. Unlike the earlier examples, these results are usually used for locating rather than editing: read `range.RangeAddress` inside the loop to get the cell reference, then act on it. A common follow-up is deleting the whole row:



    cr = sheet.FindString("Address", False, False)
    sheet.DeleteRow(cr.Row)


`FindString()` returns only the first match, which suits "handle it once" cases. Read the `Row` property from the result and pass it to `DeleteRow()` to remove the row that carries the keyword.

##  Applying a New Style During Replacement

When a replacement also has to update appearance, `ReplaceAll()` performs the content and style swap in a single call. It takes four arguments: the old text, the old style, the new text, and the new style.



    newStyle = workbook.Styles.Add("newStyle")
    newStyle.Font.FontName = "Arial Black"
    newStyle.Font.Size = 14

    cellRange = sheet.Range["D9"]
    oldStyle = cellRange.Style
    sheet.ReplaceAll("North America", oldStyle, "America", newStyle)


This replaces "North America" with "America" only in cells whose style matches cell `D9`, and applies `newStyle` (Arial Black, size 14) at the same time. Styles created with `workbook.Styles.Add()` can be reused, so for consistently formatted reports you can take the style from one sample cell and let `ReplaceAll()` filter by it, which avoids rewriting identical text elsewhere in the sheet.

##  Practical Tips

  * **Choose the match strength deliberately** : start with `False, False` to see the full set of matches, then tighten to a whole-word match once the data is confirmed clean.
  * **Log the addresses** : collect `range.RangeAddress` into a list or a log file during the loop to produce a change list after the replacement finishes.
  * **Keep a backup** : even though the script writes a new file, retain the original so the diff between the two versions stays available.
  * **Release resources** : call `workbook.Dispose()` after each workbook, and in batch jobs load, process, and release one file at a time.
  * **Work across worksheets** : `FindAllString()` operates on one worksheet, so for multi-sheet workbooks loop with `Worksheets.Count` and `get_Item(i)`.



##  Conclusion

This article covered several ways to find and replace data in Excel with Python: replacing text through `FindAllString()` and marking the results with `Style.Color`, matching complex patterns through the regex overload, locating numbers and formulas with `FindAllNumber()` and `FindAll()`, and applying a new style during replacement with `ReplaceAll()`. Combined, these operations form an auditable report-cleaning routine in which replacement and annotation happen in one pass.

We have officially entered the era of "vibe coding". You type a prompt into Cursor or Claude Code, watch hundreds of lines of polished TypeScript or Python scroll past, eye the green test suite, and hit merge. Engineering velocity has never looked higher on paper. Features that once took weeks now take hours, and product managers are celebrating unprecedented delivery metrics.

But behind the shiny dashboard numbers, senior architects and core maintainers are starting to sound an alarm.

A silent, structural decay is creeping into modern software repositories: Synthetic Code Rot. It isn't obvious at first. The tests pass, the linter doesn't complain, and the code compiles without warnings. Yet under the hood, system intuition is evaporating, micro-abstractions are multiplying exponentially, and production debugging is transforming into a high-stakes guessing game.

Here is a look at how AI-first generation is quietly degrading long-term codebases—and the concrete engineering guardrails you can deploy today to stop it.

**1. The Velocity Illusion vs. The Mental Model Deficit**
Traditionally, writing code was the slowest part of software engineering. The real work happened prior: mapping out state transitions, considering failure modes, and mental-modeling how a new feature interacted with legacy modules. Writing the actual lines was simply translating an already-formed mental model into syntax.

When you outsource the syntax generation entirely to Large Language Models (LLMs), you skip the mental modeling phase altogether.

**[ Traditional Flow ]
**Problem -> Mental Model -> Architectural Trade-offs -> Code -> Verification

**[ Vibe Coding Flow ]**
Problem -> LLM Prompt -> Eyeball Code -> Pass Tests -> Merge
The consequence? Zero institutional memory.

When an outage strikes at 2:00 AM, the engineer on call is no longer stepping through code they once conceptualized. They are staring at hundreds of lines of synthetic logic that looks right, but that no living person on the team truly understands.

**2. The "Synthetic Pattern" Problem: Over-Defensive Bloat**
LLMs are probabilistic engines trained on vast, heterogeneous open-source datasets. To minimize error rates across diverse contexts, AI code assistants exhibit distinct default behaviors that compound over time:

Micro-Abstraction Sprawl: LLMs love wrappers, helper utilities, and single-use factory functions. Instead of writing a straightforward 5-line inline function, an AI assistant will often introduce an abstract handler class, an interface, and a dependency-injected builder pattern.

Duplicated Logical Fragments: Because the LLM’s context window lacks full global awareness of your repository’s existing utility modules, it frequently re-invents minor utility logic (e.g., date formatting, string normalization, custom retry handlers) using slightly different syntax across multiple files.

Over-Defensive Null Checks & Try-Catch Bloat: LLMs frequently wrap code in excessive, generic try-catch blocks that swallow specific exceptions or return broad null values, obscuring true stack traces when silent failures occur downstream.

Individually, these patterns appear harmless. At scale, they cause code inflation—increasing the surface area of your codebase without adding real business value.

**3. The Test Suite False Sense of Security**
"If the unit tests pass, we're safe to deploy."

This classic engineering rule breaks down when AI is used to write both the implementation logic and the test suite.

LLMs naturally mirror the assumptions made in the code they generate. If an AI assistant implements a buggy state transition, it will almost certainly write a unit test that validates that specific flawed assumption. The result is a green pipeline masking fundamental edge-case vulnerabilities, race conditions, and memory leaks that only reveal themselves under real-world production load.

**4. Engineering Guardrails: How to Reclaim Control**
You don't need to ban AI coding assistants; doing so would be a massive step backward for productivity. Instead, engineering teams must transition from AI-first writing to strict AI-first auditing.

Here are four concrete strategies top engineering organizations are deploying:

A. Implement Strict AST-Based Linters & .cursorrules / Custom System Prompts
Don't rely on human reviewers to catch synthetic boilerplate. Configure AST-based linters (like ESLint rules or custom static analysis) and repo-level AI rules (.cursorrules or .claudecode guidelines) to explicitly restrict unnecessary pattern expansion:

Enforce explicit limits on file length and cyclomatic complexity.

Ban single-use factory functions and premature interface abstractions.

Mandate the reuse of verified internal utility libraries over inline generation.

B. Enforce the "Explain-the-State-Machine" PR Rule
In pull requests containing significant AI-generated logic, require the author to include a concise description of:

The underlying state transitions being modified.

Potential failure modes and how they are handled.

Why existing codebase utilities were not reused.

If the author cannot explain the exact state flow without re-prompting the AI, the PR should not pass review.

C. Separate Code Generation from Test Generation
Never let the same LLM context generate both the feature implementation and its test coverage in a single prompt. Have one engineer (or prompt run) write the implementation, and a separate test run—or ideally, a human developer—write boundary-condition tests against the spec before looking at the synthetic code.

Conclusion: Velocity is Vanity, Maintainability is Scale
AI assistants are extraordinary force multipliers for developers who already possess strong system design fundamentals. But when velocity completely untethers itself from comprehension, technical debt accumulates at compound interest.

The teams that win in the AI era won't be the ones shipping the highest volume of raw syntax—they will be the ones maintaining the crispest mental models, tightest guardrails, and cleanest architectural boundaries.

After years of web development with Firefox, these are the extensions that actually improve my workflow — not the ones that just look good in a list.

##  Privacy + Ad Blocking

###  uBlock Origin (Essential)

The only ad blocker that works exactly as advertised. Open source, maintained by Raymond Hill (gorhill), does what it says without any adware-style behavior.

Key feature for developers: **Medium Mode** (dynamic filtering). Right-click the extension popup → Dashboard → "I am an advanced user." This lets you block entire categories of third-party scripts — useful for checking what a site loads without your usual content block.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/ublock-origin

###  Multi-Account Containers (Mozilla)

First-party isolation done right. Separate sessions for work Gmail, personal Gmail, different AWS accounts — all in one browser window.

For developers: use a container for each project's staging environment. No cross-cookie leakage between environments.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/multi-account-containers

##  Session and Tab Management

###  Tab Manager & Session Saver

Named sessions for context switching. Save your "Code Review" tabs separately from "Documentation" and "Project X" tabs. One-click to switch between sets.

Key feature: all local, no cloud sync, MIT licensed. For developers who context-switch between multiple projects throughout the day.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/tab-manager-session-saver

##  Developer Tools Additions

###  Wappalyzer

Identifies technologies used by any website. Stack fingerprinting — see which framework, CDN, analytics, etc. a site uses. Useful for competitive research and inspiration.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/wappalyzer

###  JSON Formatter

Firefox displays raw JSON in the browser with no formatting. This extension formats it with collapsible trees, links, and color coding. Essential when working with APIs.

Search "JSON Formatter" on AMO — several good ones available.

###  CSS Peeper

A simplified CSS viewer for design inspection. Shows colors, fonts, and spacing of selected elements in a clean sidebar. Useful when you want quick visual inspection without opening DevTools.

##  Productivity

###  Vimium

Keyboard-driven browser navigation. `f` to show link hints, `H`/`L` for back/forward, `j`/`k` for scrolling, `T` to search open tabs, `b` for bookmarks. Takes a few days to build muscle memory but significantly reduces mouse usage.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/vimium-ff

###  Dark Reader (vs NightOwl)

**Dark Reader** : Transforms any site to dark mode via DOM manipulation. Works everywhere. Higher CPU. Occasional visual glitches.

**NightOwl** : Uses CSS `prefers-color-scheme` only. Works on sites with built-in dark mode (GitHub, HN, Notion, etc.). Lighter, less likely to break things.

If you primarily use modern developer sites: NightOwl. If you need dark mode everywhere: Dark Reader.

###  OneTab (or Tab Manager alternatives)

OneTab collapses all tabs into a list. Tab Manager & Session Saver is a more capable alternative (named sessions, restore specific sessions, not just "collapse everything").

##  Code-Related

###  Stylus

Inject custom CSS into any site. Useful for fixing a site's layout that bothers you, creating a custom reading mode for specific documentation sites, or applying company style guide tweaks.

###  Redirector

Redirect URLs automatically. Useful for always accessing a specific environment (dev vs staging vs production) or using alternative frontends for privacy.

###  PrivacyBadger (EFF)

Behavioral tracking protection. Unlike uBlock which uses lists, Privacy Badger learns over time what behaves like a tracker. Complementary to uBlock, not a replacement.

##  What I Don't Use

**Grammarly** : Sends your text to external servers. Too much privacy risk for code review comments. Use the VS Code extension instead.

**LastPass/other cloud password managers with unknown server-side access** : Bitwarden is the exception — open source, self-hostable, well-audited.

**Tab suspenders** : Modern Firefox with `browser.tabs.unloadOnLowMemory = true` handles this natively.

Start with uBlock Origin + Multi-Account Containers — these two change your browsing fundamentally. Add Tab Manager & Session Saver if you context-switch between multiple projects. Vimium if you want to go keyboard-first. Everything else is preference.

Behavioral tracking protection. Unlike uBlock which uses lists, Privacy Badger learns over time what behaves like a tracker. Complementary to uBlock, not a replacement.

What I Don't Use

Grammarly: Sends your text to external servers. Too much privacy risk for code review comments. Use the VS Code extension instead.

LastPass/other cloud password managers with unknown server-side access: Bitwarden is the exception — open source, self-hostable, well-audited.

Tab suspenders: Modern Firefox with browser.tabs.unloadOnLowMemory = true handles this natively.

Start with uBlock Origin + Multi-Account Containers — these two change your browsing fundamentally. Add Tab Manager & Session Saver if you context-switch between multiple projects. Vimium if you want to go keyboard-first. Everything else is preference.

external.description:
After years of web development with Firefox, these are the extensions that actually improve my workflow — not the ones that just look good in a list.

##  Privacy + Ad Blocking

###  uBlock Origin (Essential)

The only ad blocker that works exactly as advertised. Open source, maintained by Raymond Hill (gorhill), does what it says without any adware-style behavior.

Key feature for developers: **Medium Mode** (dynamic filtering). Right-click the extension popup → Dashboard → "I am an advanced user." This lets you block entire categories of third-party scripts — useful for checking what a site loads without your usual content block.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/ublock-origin

###  Multi-Account Containers (Mozilla)

First-party isolation done right. Separate sessions for work Gmail, personal Gmail, different AWS accounts — all in one browser window.

For developers: use a container for each project's staging environment. No cross-cookie leakage between environments.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/multi-account-containers

##  Session and Tab Management

###  Tab Manager & Session Saver

Named sessions for context switching. Save your "Code Review" tabs separately from "Documentation" and "Project X" tabs. One-click to switch between sets.

Key feature: all local, no cloud sync, MIT licensed. For developers who context-switch between multiple projects throughout the day.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/tab-manager-session-saver

##  Developer Tools Additions

###  Wappalyzer

Identifies technologies used by any website. Stack fingerprinting — see which framework, CDN, analytics, etc. a site uses. Useful for competitive research and inspiration.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/wappalyzer

###  JSON Formatter

Firefox displays raw JSON in the browser with no formatting. This extension formats it with collapsible trees, links, and color coding. Essential when working with APIs.

Search "JSON Formatter" on AMO — several good ones available.

###  CSS Peeper

A simplified CSS viewer for design inspection. Shows colors, fonts, and spacing of selected elements in a clean sidebar. Useful when you want quick visual inspection without opening DevTools.

##  Productivity

###  Vimium

Keyboard-driven browser navigation. `f` to show link hints, `H`/`L` for back/forward, `j`/`k` for scrolling, `T` to search open tabs, `b` for bookmarks. Takes a few days to build muscle memory but significantly reduces mouse usage.

Install: addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/vimium-ff

###  Dark Reader (vs NightOwl)

**Dark Reader** : Transforms any site to dark mode via DOM manipulation. Works everywhere. Higher CPU. Occasional visual glitches.

**NightOwl** : Uses CSS `prefers-color-scheme` only. Works on sites with built-in dark mode (GitHub, HN, Notion, etc.). Lighter, less likely to break things.

If you primarily use modern developer sites: NightOwl. If you need dark mode everywhere: Dark Reader.

###  OneTab (or Tab Manager alternatives)

OneTab collapses all tabs into a list. Tab Manager & Session Saver is a more capable alternative (named sessions, restore specific sessions, not just "collapse everything").

##  Code-Related

###  Stylus

Inject custom CSS into any site. Useful for fixing a site's layout that bothers you, creating a custom reading mode for specific documentation sites, or applying company style guide tweaks.

###  Redirector

Redirect URLs automatically. Useful for always accessing a specific environment (dev vs staging vs production) or using alternative frontends for privacy.

###  PrivacyBadger (EFF)

Behavioral tracking protection. Unlike uBlock which uses lists, Privacy Badger learns over time what behaves like a tracker. Complementary to uBlock, not a replacement.

##  What I Don't Use

**Grammarly** : Sends your text to external servers. Too much privacy risk for code review comments. Use the VS Code extension instead.

**LastPass/other cloud password managers with unknown server-side access** : Bitwarden is the exception — open source, self-hostable, well-audited.

**Tab suspenders** : Modern Firefox with `browser.tabs.unloadOnLowMemory = true` handles this natively.

Start with uBlock Origin + Multi-Account Containers — these two change your browsing fundamentally. Add Tab Manager & Session Saver if you context-switch between multiple projects. Vimium if you want to go keyboard-first. Everything else is preference.

▼Read More
https://tech-matome.com/archives/50766

external.description: An international research team published a paper on carbon storage in the Arctic and Southern Oceans, which account for about 20% of the Earth's oceans. Polar regions feature diverse carbon cycling pathways beyond salt marshes and seagrass beds, including macroalgae, sea ice, and fjord sediments. However, due to a lack of data on distribution, storage, and human impact, they are undervalued in climate policies. Amid increasing human activities like shipping and fishing, the team calls for standardized measurement methods and observation of entire migration pathways, urging the precautionary protection of vulnerable polar ecosystems and vast carbon reserves using existing frameworks like biodiversity frameworks and international agreements.

Auf geht’s in eine wieder mal modelllastige 42. Kalenderwoche im Jahre 2026.

## Decision 3.0

Die Meldung zu Decision 2.0 ist gerade mal eine Woche alt, und zack: Decision 3.0. Zwischen den beiden Releases lagen genau acht Tage, vom 3. bis zum 11. Oktober. Wie die Leute hinter dem vLLM Semantic Router ihre Versionierung halten, ist ihre Sache, aber man kann es auch ein wenig übertreiben.

Und was hat sich außer der Versionsnummer so geändert?

Inhaltlich rechtfertigt der Sprung die neue Hauptversion durchaus. Decision 2.0 war im Kern eine Text- und JSON-Familie für typisierte Entscheidungen. Decision 3.0 macht daraus ein multimodales Decision Model, bei dem Text, JSON, mehrere Bilder und mehrere Videos gemeinsam als State dienen können. Die drei Entscheidungstypen bleiben unverändert: Choice, Yes/No und Score, jeweils mit Wahrscheinlichkeiten und ohne generierten Freitext. Spannend ist das Kontextfenster. Der D3-Decision-Layer setzt kein eigenes `max_length`, die theoretische Obergrenze liegt damit bei den **262.144 Tokens** der zugrunde liegenden Qwen-Modelle. Öffentlich getestet hat das Team nur bis 32.000 Tokens, eine Zusage für die volle Länge ist das damit nicht.

Merkmal| Unterschied
---|---
**Grundidee**| **2.0:** Foundation Decision Model
**3.0:** Multimodal Foundation Decision Model
**Input 2.0**|  Text oder JSON
**Input 3.0**|  Text oder JSON **plus Bilder und Videos**
**Decision Types**|  Bei beiden: **Choice · Yes/No · Score**
**Output**|  Bei beiden **Wahrscheinlichkeiten für die möglichen Antworten** , keine Textgenerierung
**Mehrere Fragen – 2.0**|  Mehrere Fragen zum selben State werden **in einem Forward Pass gemeinsam** beantwortet
**Mehrere Fragen – 3.0**|  Ein API-Call kann weiterhin viele Fragen enthalten, intern bekommt aber **jede Frage einen eigenen Forward Pass** (Bilder und Videos werden nur einmal gelesen)
**Decision Head 3.0**|  Code-Readout: bis zu **255 Answer Codes** , FP32-Readout auf dem letzten Hidden State
**Varianten 3.0**|  Sechs Größen von _d3-edge_ (0,59B) bis _d3_ (26B)
**Backbones 3.0**|  Qwen3.5 von 0,8B bis 9B, **Qwen3.8-27B** für das große _d3_
**Lizenz**| **Apache 2.0**

Die Benchmarks in den Model Cards stammen vom öffentlichen Jev Decision Index, gemessen hat das Team selbst. Im unabhängigen Decision Index von Artificial Analysis (dazu gleich mehr bei _d1-ultra_) taucht Decision 3.0 noch nicht auf.

## Microsoft-Decision-1

Aber natürlich: Kaum werden Decision Models interessant, steht ein paar Wochen nach Jev auch Microsoft vor der Tür. Microsoft-Decision-1 ist am 9. Oktober erschienen und soll Routing, Klassifikation, Priorisierung, Verifikation oder Gates in Agent-Workflows übernehmen. Das Modell bekommt feste Antwortoptionen und liefert dafür Wahrscheinlichkeiten zurück, Text generiert es keinen – man kennt das mittlerweile. Unter der Haube steckt zunächst kein neues Microsoft-Basismodell. Microsoft hat für diesen Zweck ein Qwen3.5-9B post-trainiert und will es demnächst auch auf MAI- und OpenAI-Modelle umziehen. Das Kontextfenster liegt laut OpenRouter bei 32.768 Tokens, und rein darf nur Text. Der Preis beträgt 0,042 $ pro Million Input-Tokens, Output ist kostenlos (exakt der _Jev_ -Preis). Zu haben ist das Modell über Microsoft Foundry, OpenRouter und Vercels AI Gateway.

Microsoft meldet erwartungsgemäß Bestwerte aus eigenen Evals, genauer bei Genauigkeit und Tempo. Bei der Kalibrierung reicht es auch laut Microsoft nur für Platz drei, 1,5 Punkte hinter _Jev_. Die relevante Fußnote steht gleich oben im Beitrag: dieser wurde nach der Veröffentlichung aktualisiert, um _Jev_ in den Accuracy- und Calibration-Vergleich aufzunehmen. In der Urfassung vom 9. Oktober stand _Jev_ nur mit seiner Latenz in der Grafik, und Microsoft lag bei der Kalibrierung dort noch auf Platz zwei. Der naheliegendste Konkurrent hat es also erst in Version zwei des Blogposts in alle Charts geschafft, prompt rutscht Microsoft einen Platz nach hinten. Läuft.

Ein unabhängiger kleiner Reranking-Test (NFCorpus, 200 Fragen) sieht _Microsoft-Decision-1_ denn auch nicht schlecht, aber keineswegs als Durchmarsch. Je nach Setup liegt es ungefähr gleichauf mit OpenAIs Decisions API mit GPT-6 Luna und beim Reranking mit Fusion leicht hinter _Jev_. Bei Artificial Analysis landet es mit 53,8 Punkten hinter beiden _Jev_ -Versionen.

## Jev 1.14: jetzt mit Bildern

Am 14. Oktober ist bei TypeSafe Jev 1.14 hinten rausgefallen. Kleinere Verbesserungen über mehrere Bereiche, den größten Sprung erwartet TypeSafe bei mehrsprachigen Aufgaben (erwartet, wohlgemerkt). Dazu gibt es drei experimentelle Funktionen: _Jev_ verarbeitet Bilder als Input, lokalisiert mit dem neuen box-Typ Objekte darin als Bounding Box und kann deutlich längeren Context nutzen. Kleine Überraschung am Rande, Bilder und Long Context laufen auch schon mit 1.13, das Modell war laut TypeSafe „multimodal all along“. Wirklich an 1.14 gebunden ist nur box. Freigeschaltet wird das Ganze über zwei Danger-Zone-Header, einen für Bilder und box, einen für den langen Context (262.000 statt 64.000 Tokens pro Request).

Den Namen serviert TypeSafe mit reichlich Emojis, dahinter steckt trotzdem eine brauchbare Produktentscheidung. Denn TypeSafe sagt selbst deutlich, dass diese Funktionen nicht für Production gedacht sind:

> we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!

Multimodalität sei weniger zuverlässig als reiner Text, und auch längerer Context verschlechtere die Zuverlässigkeit. Besonders interessant finde ich box. Damit geht _Jev_ erstmals über reine probabilistische Entscheidungen à la „ja/nein“ oder „Option A/B/C“ hinaus und liefert eine strukturierte Position innerhalb eines Bildes zurück, vier Kanten plus Confidence. Eine Antwort „nicht gefunden“ kennt box nicht, dafür soll man zusätzlich eine Ja/Nein-Frage stellen. Das öffnet neue Workflows, am eigentlichen Konzept ändert es nichts. _Jev_ bleibt ein Werkzeug für kleine, typisierte Entscheidungen in Software, und Modelle, die einem einen Aufsatz schreiben, gibt es ja genug.

TypeSafe veröffentlicht dazu auch neue interne Messungen. Die würde ich vorerst genau dort einsortieren – interne Messungen. Das Unternehmen weist immerhin selbst darauf hin, dass sich die Eval-Methode noch verändert und zugunsten des eigenen Modells verzerrt sein kann („This is likely biased towards our models.“). Fair enough. Artificial Analysis sieht 1.14 mit 57,1 Punkten sogar minimal unter 1.13 (57,5), dafür flotter. Für mich zeigt _Jev 1.14_ deshalb vor allem, wohin TypeSafe mit seinen System-One-Modellen will: mehr Input-Typen und mehr mögliche Entscheidungen, ohne aus _Jev_ heimlich doch noch ein LLM für alles zu machen. Der Preis bleibt bei 0,042 $ pro Million Input-Tokens, `jev-latest` soll in rund einer Woche auf 1.14 umspringen.

## Liquid AI d1-ultra

Inzwischen wird es bei den Decision Models richtig voll. Liquid AI hat am 15. Oktober mit d1-ultra die leistungsfähigere Variante seiner d1-Familie nachgelegt. Das Prinzip bleibt gleich. Text und Bilder rein, eine oder mehrere vorgegebene Fragen dazu, und das Modell liefert in einem Forward Pass Wahrscheinlichkeiten für noul (so heißt Ja/Nein im System-One-Format von TypeSafe), choice oder score. Keine generierten Antworten, keine Output-Tokens. Liquid verlangt 0,042 $ pro Million Input-Tokens, womit sich bei TypeSafe, Microsoft und Liquid offenbar ein Einheitspreis eingependelt hat.

Multimodal waren schon die kleinen d1-Modelle, mit _d1-ultra_ kommt das in die größere Klasse (siehe auch den Pick zu _Jev 1.14_). Damit lässt sich etwa entscheiden, wohin ein Support-Ticket gehört, genauso aber, ob ein Bauteil auf einem Foto einen Defekt hat oder eine Schadensmeldung zum Bild des Kunden passt. Gebaut hat Liquid _d1-ultra_ auf Basis eines größeren Open-Weight-Modells (welches, verrät Liquid nicht) und es stark angepasst. Die Gewichte von _d1-ultra_ selbst gibt es trotzdem nicht. Es gibt das Modell über die Liquid API und, anders als im Blog noch angekündigt, schon jetzt auch bei OpenRouter und im Vercel AI Gateway, jeweils mit 32.768 Tokens Kontext.

Wichtig für die Preisliste im Hinterkopf: Jede Frage wird als eigener Prompt inklusive State und aller Bilder berechnet. Ein Bild mit 1.024 × 1.024 Pixeln kostet 1.536 Tokens, bei drei Fragen fallen damit mindestens 4.608 Bild-Tokens an, dazu dreimal State und Fragetext. Bei 0,042 $ pro Million fällt das erst bei großem Volumen ins Gewicht, aber genau da wollen solche Modelle ja hin. Bei _Jev_ wird ein Bild im State übrigens nur einmal für alle Fragen gelesen.

Mit dem Artificial Analysis Decision Index gibt es seit dem 13. Oktober auch einen unabhängigen Benchmark speziell für diese Modellklasse. Er prüft zu gleichen Teilen Klassifikation (WildGuardTest), Tool-Calling (When2Call), Wissen und Halluzinationen (AA-Omniscience) sowie Reasoning (Fragen aus Humanity’s Last Exam). Der aktuelle Stand für die Modelle aus diesen und den letzten Picks:

  * _d1-ultra_ : 65,2
  *  _Jev 1.13_ : 57,5 und _Jev 1.14_ : 57,1
  *  _Microsoft-Decision-1_ : 53,8
  * Clef: 48,6
  *  _GPT-6 Luna_ (Decisions API): 48,5



Liquids Sieg ist deutlich, bloß der Claim „outperforms Jev 1.14 across all tasks“ hält nicht ganz. Bei Reasoning und Wissensgenauigkeit liegt _Jev_ vorn, der Vorsprung von _d1-ultra_ kommt vor allem vom ehrlichen „Ich weiß es nicht“ (Non-Hallucination-Rate 84,5 gegenüber 37,2) und vom Tool-Calling. Zur Einordnung der ganzen Klasse hilft ein Blick auf die LLMs im selben Index. Claude Haiku 5.5 auf Max kommt auf 68,4. Decision Models gewinnen bei Preis und Tempo, bei Wissen und Reasoning liegen ordentliche LLMs weiter vorn – das kommt von Artificial Analysis selbst.

InclusionAI aus dem Umfeld der Ant Group hat die Gewichte von Ling-3.1-flash am 14. Oktober unter MIT-Lizenz veröffentlicht. Die FP8-Weights liegen inzwischen auf Hugging Face, knapp 574 GB fett, empfohlen wird ein SGLang-Setup auf 8 × H200. „Open“ heißt bei 560B also eher Rechenzentrum als bessere Bürokiste. Wer es lieber gehostet mag, zahlt bei OpenRouter derzeit 0,075 $ / 0,225 $ pro Million Input-/Output-Tokens (75 % Aktionsrabatt auf 0,30 $ / 0,90 $). ## Nemotron 3.5 Super VL und Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B

Am 15. Oktober hat NVIDIA gleich zwei Modelle der Familie rausgehauen (nach Nemotron 3.5 Lightning im August): Nemotron 3.5 Super VL und Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B. Super VL ist ein multimodales 120B-MoE mit 12B aktiven Parametern, kombiniert Mamba-2, Transformer und einen C-RADIO-Vision-Encoder und verarbeitet Text, Bilder sowie Video (bis zwei Minuten) bei bis zu 1 Million Tokens Kontext. Tool Calling, Reasoning und Structured Outputs sind direkt vorgesehen. Die Gewichte gibt es in BF16 und quantisiertem NVFP4, Lizenz ist die permissive OpenMDW 1.1 der Linux Foundation.

Artificial Analysis misst 26 Punkte, doppelt so viel wie beim Vorgänger _Nemotron 3 Super_ , mit rund 60 % weniger Output-Tokens pro Task und praktisch ohne Verlust in NVFP4. NVIDIAs Effizienz-Story stammt damit nicht komplett aus der eigenen Presseabteilung, auch wenn AA das Modell im Klassenvergleich trotzdem „somewhat verbose“ nennt. Das oft zitierte „leading open model“ braucht ebenfalls sein Sternchen. Die Formulierung stammt von AA und bezog sich auf die US-Open-Weight-Kategorie, und selbst dort hielt der Titel nur ein paar Stunden, bis Meta am Abend nachlegte (siehe nächster Pick). In der Gewichtsklasse 40 bis 150 Milliarden Parameter liegt Super VL bei AA dagegen weltweit vorn.

Interessanter finde ich eigentlich Bolt: NVIDIA komprimiert Super VL auf 74B Gesamt- und 9B aktive Parameter, 256K Kontext und eine native 2-Bit-Quantisierung (genauer eine Mischung, die Experts liegen in 2 Bit, der Rest in NVFP4 und 8 Bit), sodass die Gewichte rund 24 GB wiegen. Es bleibt multimodal und unterstützt Tool Use sowie abschaltbares Thinking. NVIDIA liefert neben Safetensors gleich ein offizielles GGUF mit, Unsloth hat nachgezogen. Belegt sind llama.cpp, Ollama, Unsloth und vLLM, für LM Studio habe ich noch keinen Bolt-Eintrag gefunden. Damit wird aus dem üblichen „offene Gewichte, viel Spaß mit deinem Rechenzentrum“ tatsächlich ein Modell, das lokal auf stärkerer Consumer-Hardware interessant wird.

Mit universeller Hardware-Kompatibilität hat die 24-GB-Angabe wenig zu tun, sie beschreibt die Dateigröße. NVIDIAs Rezepte verlangen für den Betrieb 28 beziehungsweise 32 GB, das heißt eine Grafikkarte ab 32 GB oder 64 GB Unified Memory, eine RTX 4090 mit 24 GB sieht NVIDIA gar nicht vor. Der validierte Pfad ist, wenig überraschend, NVIDIA-lastig (Blackwell, Linux, RTX und DGX Spark). Bei AA landet Bolt mit 21 Punkten nur zwei hinter dem rund siebenmal größeren _Nemotron 3 Ultra_.

Wo wir gerade bei nicht ganz unerheblichen Einschränkungen sind: Mit Open Source hat das trotz offener Gewichte wenig zu tun. Technisch ist der Release trotzdem relevant. Bevor man das jetzt aber als Frontier-Modell liest, hier der kleine Dämpfer: Artificial Analysis misst 39 Punkte, das reicht für Platz eins unter den US-Open-Weight-Modellen. Metas eigenes geschlossenes Muse Wonder liegt allerdings 13 Punkte darüber. Und das chinesische _Ling-3.1-flash_ von weiter oben zieht mit 41 Punkten an Meta vorbei. So viel zum US-Sternchen.

Mit „Agentic AI auf jedem Gerät“ kann ich wenig anfangen. Spannend finde ich, dass hier 2 bis 9 Milliarden Parameter mit langem Kontext und multimodalem Input in Größenordnungen landen, bei denen lokales Deployment nicht mehr nach Homelab-Spleen klingt.

## MASS – Multi-Agent Self-Supervision

Sakana AI und Forschende der UC Berkeley (darunter Databricks-Mitgründer Matei Zaharia) stellen mit MASS – Multi-Agent Self-Supervision – einen Ansatz für Recursive Self-Improvement vor, samt Paper und Code. Die Idee: Dasselbe Modell übernimmt drei Jobs. Es löst die Aufgabe, optimiert den Multi-Agent-Workflow und bewertet anschließend die Ergebnisse im paarweisen Vergleich. Im Inner Loop bleiben die Gewichte unangetastet, optimiert wird die Organisation der Agenten mit Rollen, Instructions, Output Contracts und der Reihenfolge der Aufrufe. Die besten Workflows laufen anschließend mehrfach (18-mal pro Aufgabe), das Modell rankt die Ergebnisse selbst, und die Gewinner werden zu Trainingsdaten. Im Outer Loop landet diese Erfahrung per LoRA wieder im Modell. Dann beginnt das Spiel von vorn, im Experiment waren es zwei Runden.

Das ist beileibe spannender als das übliche „wir lassen fünf Agenten miteinander reden“. Ausgangspunkt ist _Qwen3.6-27B_ im qwen-code-Harness, und MASS versucht explizit, gute Koordination aus den Multi-Agent-Traces in die Gewichte zu destillieren. Nach zwei Runden delegiert das Modell auch ohne vorgegebenen Workflow, in 87 von 110 Läufen statt in einem einzigen. Sakana beobachtet außerdem, dass optimierte Workflows mit der Zeit weniger Information in hübschen Rollenbeschreibungen und mehr in Contracts und Übergaben zwischen den Agenten tragen. Ganz von allein kam das nicht, wie Sakana selbst einräumt, denn der System-Prompt des Optimierers schubst genau in diese Richtung. Es passt trotzdem gut zu dem, was bei produktiven Agent-Systemen ohnehin zählt (siehe auch Loop Engineering): Wer liefert wem was – und wann?

Eine Einschränkung wird gleich mitgeliefert: Das Experiment umfasst nur zwölf synthetische Research-Aufgaben aus Finance, Robotics und Pharmacy, neun davon fürs Training. Auf ähnlich gelagerten Research-Evals verbessert sich das Modell, die Hauptmetrik ist dabei Score pro Output-Token und misst eher Effizienz. Bei Software-Engineering wird es auf SWE-bench Verified und Terminal-Bench 2.0 sogar minimal schlechter. Der offensichtlichste Haken steckt im Konzept selbst. Wenn dasselbe Modell erzeugt, optimiert und bewertet, können sich gemeinsame Blind Spots gleich mitoptimieren, und Sakana benennt das selbst:

> shared blind spots may be an Achilles’ heel of recursive self-improvement.

Meinen ersten Verdacht, dass LLM-as-a-Judge durch das gleiche Modell eher kontraproduktiv ist, stützen die Daten allerdings nicht. Die Übereinstimmung des Selbst-Bewerters mit externen Judges (_GPT-5.5_ und _Claude Opus 4.8_) steigt über die Zyklen von 73 auf 93 %, und laut Paper ist eher der Optimierer der Engpass als der Bewerter. Ich lasse das so stehen. MASS ist ein interessantes Forschungsstück über lernende Agent-Workflows. Ob sich Modelle demnächst zuverlässig selbst aus dem Sumpf ziehen, belegt es noch nicht.

## Claude Code Desktop App frisch renoviert für parallele Sessions

Anthropic hat der _Claude Code_ Desktop-App am 14. Oktober ein Update für paralleles Arbeiten spendiert. Sessions lassen sich schneller starten, zuletzt genutzte Ordner liegen direkt bereit, und wiederkehrende Setups aus mehreren Ordnern, einem SSH-Host oder der Cloud lassen sich als Environment speichern, auf Wunsch mit einem Worktree pro Ordner. Interessant wird es beim Aufteilen größerer Aufgaben. Wer Claude bittet, Aufgaben parallel abzuarbeiten, bekommt pro Aufgabe eine eigene verschachtelte Session, die ihr Ergebnis anschließend an die Hauptsession meldet. Von sich aus schlägt Claude Folgeaufgaben vor, die sich per Klick als eigene Session starten lassen. Sidebar, Live-To-do-Liste und Recap-Karten sollen sichtbar machen, wer gerade arbeitet und wo Claude auf den Nutzer wartet. Die Dokumentation beschreibt die Basis mit parallelen Sessions, optionalen Git-Worktrees, Cloud- und SSH-Sessions sowie Side Chats. Die Neuerungen dieser Woche stehen bislang nur im Ankündigungs-Thread.

In erster Linie ist das eine bessere Bedienoberfläche für Dinge, die darunter zum guten Teil schon existierten. Parallele Sessions, Worktrees und Side Chats sind keine Erfindung dieser Woche, Anthropic hatte die Desktop-App bereits im April auf mehrere gleichzeitige Agenten ausgerichtet. Neu ist vor allem, dass der ganze Kram stärker zusammengezogen wird und Claude die Aufteilung in weitere Sessions sichtbarer übernimmt. Fürs Terminal gab es am selben Tag übrigens Idle Compaction. Lange Sessions, die herumliegen, komprimiert _Claude Code_ jetzt kurz bevor der Prompt-Cache nach rund einer Stunde abläuft.

Und genau dieses Aufräumen finde ich an dem Update deutlich interessanter als jedes „autonome Agenten“-Marketing-Gedöns. Wenn fünf Sessions gleichzeitig werkeln, ist ein sechster Agent schnell gestartet. Schwieriger wird es, im Blick zu behalten, welcher gerade was tut, worauf er wartet und welche Änderungen am Ende wo landen. Agentic Coding bekommt langsam dasselbe Problem wie klassische Projektarbeit (siehe auch den Koordinator in den neuen Claude-Projekten). Überraschend eigentlich nur, dass wir dafür wieder bei einer GUI landen und das Terminal mal Pause hat.

## Scion: Versionierung made by Anthropic

Heise berichtet, dass Anthropic sein internes Monorepo von Git auf ein eigenes Source-Control-System namens _Scion_ umgezogen hat, die Details liefert Anthropic im Engineering-Blog gleich selbst. Den Ausschlag gibt Anthropics inzwischen ziemlich absurder Workload. Die Merges pro Tag sind von rund 2.500 im Mai auf über 30.000 im September gestiegen, die Main-History allein ist knapp 100 GB groß, und die CI checkt täglich etwa 25 Millionen Mal Code aus. Naiv per Git geholt wären das über 600 PB Traffic am Tag. _Scion_ dreht deshalb einige Git-Grundannahmen um. Clients gelten als immer online, Historie, Merges, Rebases und Blame liegen serverseitig, Working Copies sind optional, und Dateien werden sparse beziehungsweise bei Bedarf materialisiert. Die Arbeitseinheit sind serverseitige Changesets, die Daten verteilt _Scion_ horizontal über Storage und Caches.

Anthropic meldet dafür einen 200-mal kleineren CPU- und RAM-Bedarf gegenüber der vorherigen Git-Mirror-Infrastruktur, Checkouts in Sekunden statt Minuten, und in der CI wurden 25 % CPU-Kapazität frei. Das sind Anthropics eigene Zahlen aus Anthropics eigener Infrastruktur, unabhängige Messungen gibt es naturgemäß nicht. Zum Ausprobieren taugt _Scion_ auch nicht. Anthropic hält eine öffentliche Version für wenig sinnvoll, weil _Scion_ stark von Git abweicht und eigenes Code Review, eigene Code-Suche und eigene CI voraussetzt (bei Heise heißt das schlicht, Anthropic wolle es nicht veröffentlichen). Die Ideen sollen stattdessen zusammen mit GitHub, GitLab und der Open-Source-Community in Git einfließen. Was _Scion_ nicht sein soll, schreibt Anthropic unmissverständlich hin:

> Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use.

So viel zur „Git-Alternative“ aus der Heise-Überschrift.

Wenn Coding-Agenten Code schneller produzieren, als klassische CI-, Review- und Source-Control-Infrastruktur ihn verdauen kann, verschiebt sich der Flaschenhals einfach eine Etage weiter. Anthropic sieht den Engpass inzwischen selbst in der Entwickler-Infrastruktur, die für menschliches Tempo gebaut wurde, und rechnet damit, dass andere in sechs bis zwölf Monaten vor derselben Frage stehen. Für 99,x % der Teams bleibt Git deshalb das passende Werkzeug. Anthropic zeigt trotzdem ganz gut, welche Infrastrukturfragen auftauchen, wenn Agenten im industriellen Maßstab Änderungen rausfeuern, wo sie früher gelegentlich mitgecodet haben. Zed arbeitet mit Delta gerade an einer ähnlichen Baustelle.

## The X Subscription: Grok, Cursor und X Premium in einem Abo

Wer schon immer das Supidupi-Rundum-Paket haben wollte, bekommt das jetzt in einem Abo. SpaceXAI hat am 12. Oktober The X Subscription vorgestellt, die Grok, Grok Bot, _Cursor_ und X Premium unter einen Hut bringt, samt Zugang zur Grok-API (deren Nutzung wird separat zu den normalen Tokenpreisen abgerechnet). Grok Bot, Cloud Agents und Automationen, Code-Hosting über Origin und KI-Code-Reviews über Bugbot kosten keinen Aufpreis, die stecken ab der Stufe Premium mit drin.

Ernsthaft zu haben ist das Ganze ab 8 $ im Monat, alle Stufen teilen sich einen wöchentlichen Nutzungspool für _Cursor_ und Grok. Die Staffel laut Preisseite:

  * Free: 0 $, mit Tageskontingent
  * Plus: 8 $, _Cursor_ nur mit Grok-Modellen, kein Grok Bot
  * Premium: 30 $, laut SpaceXAI der Gegenwert von SuperGrok, Cursor Pro und X Premium+
  * Super: 100 $
  * Ultra: 200 $



Jährlich wird es etwas günstiger, die Preise verstehen sich ohne Steuern. Team-Optionen gibt es ab 30 $ pro Nutzer und Monat, Plus ist für Teams nicht buchbar.

Wie gut der Gegenwert des 8-Dollar-Deals bei einer halbwegs ambitionierten Nutzung von _Cursor_ ist, kann ich mangels Erfahrungswerten nicht beurteilen. Bei Plus gibt es in _Cursor_ ohnehin nur Grok-Modelle, und die „Latest Grok models“ führt die Preistabelle erst ab Premium. Das aktuelle Grok 4.7 ist im Plus-Tarif trotzdem enthalten (allerdings nur mit Medium-Effort verfügbar). Die Cursor-Preisseite empfiehlt Plus eher „social creators with limited AI usage“.

Apropos, etwas verwirrend: Auf der Website steht unten noch „© 2026 SpaceXAI LLC“, die Seitentitel tragen aber schon „SpaceXSI“, und der X-Account heißt mittlerweile trendgerecht „SpaceX Super Intelligence“.

## Gemini 4 Argon in Google Antigravity verfügbar

Google hat Gemini 4 Argon am 13. Oktober in Antigravity und der Gemini API freigeschaltet, sowohl in der Desktop-App als auch in der CLI. Am selben Tag kam das Modell auch in die Gemini-App für AI Pro und Ultra.

Google nennt über 100.000 monatliche Argon-Nutzer bei Alphabet, die mit der internen Antigravity-Version arbeiten, und berichtet über vier Wochen von 35 % mehr agentisch erzeugtem Code bei gleichzeitig 30 % weniger Rollbacks nach dem Einreichen. Das sind Zahlen aus dem eigenen Maschinenraum. Unabhängiger ist Artificial Analysis mit 53 Punkten im Intelligence Index, gleichauf mit _GPT-6 Astra_ und pro Aufgabe zum Einführungspreis rund 40 % günstiger.

Der kleine Haken beim Zugang: In _Antigravity_ bekam man Argon zunächst nur mit Google AI Ultra oder einem passenden Gemini-Enterprise-Abo (den Blogpost hat Google inzwischen still auf „Pro and Ultra“ umgeschrieben). Über die API reicht ein bezahlter Gemini-API-Account mit aktiviertem Billing, der Free Tier ist raus. Seit dem 15. Oktober (US-Zeit) darf man auch mit dem Pro-Abonnement mitspielen, mit einem eigenen wöchentlichen Argon-Kontingent.

Ach so, bei OpenRouter geht es auch ganz ohne Abo, vorerst zum bekannten Einführungspreis von 2 $ / 10 $ pro Million Input-/Output-Tokens. Das ist Googles eigener API-Preis, und der verdoppelt sich ab dem 1. Dezember auf 4 $ / 20 $.

## Google serviert Scrapern offenbar Fake-SERPs

Passt nur über Bande zum Thema KI, lustig ist es trotzdem. Google scheint erkannten Scrapern inzwischen Suchergebnisse unterzuschieben, die vollkommen normal aussehen und nur eben nicht stimmen. SEO Südwest greift dazu eine Analyse von Nozzle auf. Nozzle hat 27,5 Millionen seit dem 13. September gesammelte SERPs ausgewertet, und von den 17,8 Millionen bewertbaren galten 8 % nach Nozzles Definition als „poisoned“ (vorher waren es 0,17 %). Gewohnte Treffer verschwinden, Reddit, Facebook, LinkedIn oder Quora rücken nach, und ein Rank-Tracker speichert das Ganze brav als echten Rankingverlust. Ausgerechnet Österreich liegt mit 18,8 % vergifteter SERPs an der Spitze, Deutschland kommt auf 4,3 %.

Das Gemeine daran: Ein geblockter Scraper weiß wenigstens, dass er geblockt wurde. Eine plausibel aussehende Fake-SERP landet dagegen einfach in den Daten. Bei 77,9 % der von Nozzle erkannten Fälle waren die gewohnten Ergebnisse innerhalb von drei Tagen wieder da. Für SEO-Tools ist das unangenehm, und für deren Nutzer ein guter Grund, bei plötzlich abstürzenden Rankings erst einmal in die Search Console zu schauen, bevor jemand hektisch die halbe Website umbaut. Das empfiehlt auch Nozzle.

Nozzle hält das Ganze für Googles Antwort auf KI-Scraper, die Suchergebnisse in großem Stil für KI-Antworten einsammeln, Rank-Tracker wären demnach nur Beifang (da ist er dann doch, der KI-Bezug). Die Interpretation ist schlüssig, eine Stellungnahme von Google gibt es bislang aber nicht. Ende September lief außerdem ein Spam-Update, echte Rankingverluste sind in dem Zeitraum ebenfalls möglich. Wer gerade seine KI-Sichtbarkeit oder klassische Rankings mit Tools misst, sollte deren Datenquelle im Moment besonders kritisch anschauen.

Damit Feierabend für diese Woche – und glaubt keinem Rankingabsturz, den die Search Console nicht bestätigt.
